To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
head injury is the leading cause of hospitalization for children aged 0 -7 years in the region, and that the outcome is good in most cases.
head injury requiring hospitalisation in children is not rare.

1) the incidence of hospitalized head injury in Israeli children aged < 8 years is 1.71 per 1000 per year; 2) 50 per cent were admitted for more than 24 hours; 3) 50 per percent of those who were hospitalized were followed up for 4-10 post-injury years, and 4) the most common sequelae were neuropsychiatric symptoms, and school failure.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the incidence, etiology, and outcome of head injuries in a population of children.
the following questions: What are the characteristics of the children with the most severe head injuries?
the effects of head injury on children and adolescents.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in Israel, the incidence of head injury in childhood is high.
the outcome of head injury in childhood is not necessarily benign.
the outcome of head injury in childhood is not necessarily poor, and that the majority of these children do not develop serious sequelae.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the majority of children who sustain a head injury recover completely, but a significant proportion have long-term sequelae.
, in the long term, the most important sequelae of childhood head injuries are neuropsychiatric.

the long-term sequelae of head injury in Israeli children is not severe and is not related to severity of the initial injury, but that there is a high prevalence of various neuropsychiatric and behavioural symptoms.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the prevalence of neuropsychiatric symptoms was significantly greater than that of neurological deficits.
the majority of children with severe head injuries will have long term neuropsychiatric sequelae.
head injury can have serious long-term consequences, even in the absence of seizures or neurological deficit.
